items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate the repeated integral
[MATH: \int_{\color{black}0}^{\color{black}2} \int_{\color{black}x/2}^{\color{black}1} \, e^{y^2}\,\textrm{d}{\color{black}y} \, \textrm{d}{\color{black}x}.]

Content:
The expression "[MATH: \,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,]" tells us that we should integrate first with respect to [MATH: y.] This is problematic, though, as the integrand [MATH: e^{y^2}] does not have an elementary antiderivative. So, what can we do?

Content:
In cases like this, reversing the order of integration from [MATH: \, \textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,] to [MATH: \, \textrm{d}x\,\textrm{d}y] might help. But beware! Because the domain of integration is non-rectangular, we can't just swap the order of the integrals. This is because, to integrate with respect to [MATH: x,] we can't have [MATH: x]'s in the limits. So we need to work out new limits.

Content:
When swapping the order of integration, it is helpful to sketch the region [MATH: D] over which we're integrating.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/73648a05b2319a98900ba8a99b569ca0]

Content:
To integrate first with respect to [MATH: y,] we imagine a line parallel to the [MATH: y]-axis, as shown above. Note the following:

Content:
- This line enters the region through the curve [MATH: \color{black} y=\dfrac{x}{2}] and leaves at [MATH: \color{black} y=1.] These are the variable limits for [MATH: y.]
- The minimum value of [MATH: x] is [MATH: \color{black}0,] and the maximum value of [MATH: x] is [MATH: {\color{black}2}.]

Content:
So, the integral we were initially given is over the following type I region:

Content:
[MATH: D=\left \{ (x,y) \: : \: {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2}, \quad {\color{black}\dfrac{x}{2}} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}]

Content:
However, since we now want to integrate first with respect to [MATH: x,] we need the limits for [MATH: x] to be functions of [MATH: y], and we need the limits of [MATH: y] to be constants. To work these out, we redraw the region, but this time we imagine a line parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cd01c4808bee652491eadec84a121ae4]

Content:
- The line enters the region at [MATH: \color{black}x=0] and leaves the region at [MATH: \color{black} x=2y.] So these are our variable limits for [MATH: x.]
- The minimum value of [MATH: \color{black}y] is [MATH: \color{black}0,] and the maximum value of [MATH: y] is [MATH: {\color{black}1}.]

Content:
So, we can consider [MATH: D] to be the following type II region:

Content:
[MATH: D=\left \{ (x,y):\quad {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2y}, \quad {\color{black}0} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}]

Content:
Now that we have expressed the region [MATH: D] as a type II region, we're ready to swap the order of integration and finally calculate our integral:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{2}∫_{x/2}^{1}e^{y^{2}}dydx|= ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{2y}e^{y^{2}}dxdy; = ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y^{2}}[∫_{0}^{2y}dx]dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y^{2}}[x]_{0}^{2y}dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}2ye^{y^{2}}dy; = [e^{y^{2}}]_{0}^{1}; = e − 1.]

sections.readable_text:
Change the order of integration in the double integral
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_{y^3}^{1} f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

[MATH: D= \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq1, \quad y^3 \leq x \leq 1 \big\},]

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form [MATH: x=x(y),] is

[MATH: x = y^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y = \sqrt[3]{x},]

and the bottom boundary of the region is

[MATH: y = 0.]

To change the order of integration, we write [MATH: D] as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

[MATH: D= \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt[3]{x} \big\}.]

as shown in the diagram below.

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{y^{3}}^{1}f(x, y)dxdy|= ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{root(x, 3)}f(x, y)dydx.]

items.title: Swapping the Order of Integration on a Partitioned Region

sections.normalized_html: Change the order of integration in the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^1\int_{2x}^{3-x} f(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x .]
sections.readable_text: Change the order of integration in the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^1\int_{2x}^{3-x} f(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x .]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

[MATH: D=\big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 2x \leq y \leq 3-x \big\}.]

To change the order of integration, we need to split [MATH: D] into two type II regions.

Notice that the right boundary of the lower region, written in the form [MATH: x=x(y),] is [MATH: x=\dfrac{y}{2}.]

Also, the right boundary of the upper region, written in the form [MATH: x=x(y),] is [MATH: x=3-y.]

So, we can write [MATH: D] as a union of

[MATH: D_1 = \Big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq 2, \quad 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{y}{2} \Big\}]

and

[MATH: D_2 = \Big\{ (x,y) \::\: 2 \leq y \leq 3, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 3-y \Big\}.]

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{2x}^{3 − x}f(x, y)dydx|= ∫_{0}^{2}∫_{0}^{y/2}f(x, y)dxdy + ∫_{2}^{3}∫_{0}^{3 − y}f(x, y)dxdy.]

sections.normalized_html: Change the order of integration and evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle{\int_0^{1} \int_{\sqrt{x}}^{1 } 9\sqrt{y^3+1}\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x}.]
sections.readable_text: Change the order of integration and evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle{\int_0^{1} \int_{\sqrt{x}}^{1 } 9\sqrt{y^3+1}\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

[MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad \sqrt{x} \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.]

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form [MATH: y=y(x),] is

[MATH: x=0,]

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form [MATH: y=y(x),] is

[MATH: y = \sqrt{x} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=y^2.]

To change the order of integration, we write [MATH: D] as type II region. Its type II representation is

[MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y^2 \big\},]

as shown in the diagram below.

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{sqrt(x)}^{1}9sqrt(y^{3} + 1)dydx|= ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{y^{2}}9sqrt(y^{3} + 1)dxdy; = 9∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(y^{3} + 1)[∫_{0}^{y^{2}}dx]dy; = 9∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(y^{3} + 1)[x]_{0}^{y^{2}}dy; = 3∫_{0}^{1}3y^{2}(y^{3} + 1)^{1/2}dy; = 3[(2)/(3)(y^{3} + 1)^{3/2}]_{0}^{1}; = [2(y^{3} + 1)^{3/2}]_{0}^{1}; = 2(2)^{3/2} − 2; = 4sqrt(2) − 2.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate the repeated integral
[MATH: \int_{\color{black}0}^{\color{black}2} \int_{\color{black}x/2}^{\color{black}1} \, e^{y^2}\,\textrm{d}{\color{black}y} \, \textrm{d}{\color{black}x}.]

Content:
The expression "[MATH: \,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,]" tells us that we should integrate first with respect to [MATH: y.] This is problematic, though, as the integrand [MATH: e^{y^2}] does not have an elementary antiderivative. So, what can we do?

Content:
In cases like this, reversing the order of integration from [MATH: \, \textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,] to [MATH: \, \textrm{d}x\,\textrm{d}y] might help. But beware! Because the domain of integration is non-rectangular, we can't just swap the order of the integrals. This is because, to integrate with respect to [MATH: x,] we can't have [MATH: x]'s in the limits. So we need to work out new limits.

Content:
When swapping the order of integration, it is helpful to sketch the region [MATH: D] over which we're integrating.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/73648a05b2319a98900ba8a99b569ca0]

Content:
To integrate first with respect to [MATH: y,] we imagine a line parallel to the [MATH: y]-axis, as shown above. Note the following:

Content:
- This line enters the region through the curve [MATH: \color{black} y=\dfrac{x}{2}] and leaves at [MATH: \color{black} y=1.] These are the variable limits for [MATH: y.]
- The minimum value of [MATH: x] is [MATH: \color{black}0,] and the maximum value of [MATH: x] is [MATH: {\color{black}2}.]

Content:
So, the integral we were initially given is over the following type I region:

Content:
[MATH: D=\left \{ (x,y) \: : \: {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2}, \quad {\color{black}\dfrac{x}{2}} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}]

Content:
However, since we now want to integrate first with respect to [MATH: x,] we need the limits for [MATH: x] to be functions of [MATH: y], and we need the limits of [MATH: y] to be constants. To work these out, we redraw the region, but this time we imagine a line parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cd01c4808bee652491eadec84a121ae4]

Content:
- The line enters the region at [MATH: \color{black}x=0] and leaves the region at [MATH: \color{black} x=2y.] So these are our variable limits for [MATH: x.]
- The minimum value of [MATH: \color{black}y] is [MATH: \color{black}0,] and the maximum value of [MATH: y] is [MATH: {\color{black}1}.]

Content:
So, we can consider [MATH: D] to be the following type II region:

Content:
[MATH: D=\left \{ (x,y):\quad {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2y}, \quad {\color{black}0} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}]

Content:
Now that we have expressed the region [MATH: D] as a type II region, we're ready to swap the order of integration and finally calculate our integral:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{2}∫_{x/2}^{1}e^{y^{2}}dydx|= ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{2y}e^{y^{2}}dxdy; = ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y^{2}}[∫_{0}^{2y}dx]dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y^{2}}[x]_{0}^{2y}dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}2ye^{y^{2}}dy; = [e^{y^{2}}]_{0}^{1}; = e − 1.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Swapping the Order of Integration on a Non-Partitioned Region

Example Prompt:
Change the order of integration in the double integral
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_{y^3}^{1} f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
[IMG: /graphics/25d522dde8ecc0a0a3957dae03108ac8]

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

[MATH: D= \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq1, \quad y^3 \leq x \leq 1 \big\},]

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form [MATH: x=x(y),] is

[MATH: x = y^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y = \sqrt[3]{x},]

and the bottom boundary of the region is

[MATH: y = 0.]

To change the order of integration, we write [MATH: D] as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

[MATH: D= \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt[3]{x} \big\}.]

as shown in the diagram below.

[IMG: /graphics/925312e310acb44953022570595a9942]

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{y^{3}}^{1}f(x, y)dxdy|= ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{root(x, 3)}f(x, y)dydx.]

---

Item 5 — Example: Swapping the Order of Integration on a Partitioned Region

Example Prompt:
Change the order of integration in the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^1\int_{2x}^{3-x} f(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x .]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
[IMG: /graphics/d5f8a21d03c9e61e36a15cd45faecbfa]

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

[MATH: D=\big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 2x \leq y \leq 3-x \big\}.]

To change the order of integration, we need to split [MATH: D] into two type II regions.

[IMG: /graphics/4e6985e72db38bb32ef0c05926b8ba59]

Notice that the right boundary of the lower region, written in the form [MATH: x=x(y),] is
[MATH: x=\dfrac{y}{2}.]

Also, the right boundary of the upper region, written in the form [MATH: x=x(y),] is
[MATH: x=3-y.]

So, we can write [MATH: D] as a union of

[MATH: D_1 = \Big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq 2, \quad 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{y}{2} \Big\}]

and

[MATH: D_2 = \Big\{ (x,y) \::\: 2 \leq y \leq 3, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 3-y \Big\}.]

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{2x}^{3 − x}f(x, y)dydx|= ∫_{0}^{2}∫_{0}^{y/2}f(x, y)dxdy + ∫_{2}^{3}∫_{0}^{3 − y}f(x, y)dxdy.]
